q0_0_3_0:
Virchow's Triad & Thrombosis

Rudolf Virchow (1856) proposed that thrombosis results from a disturbance in three factors — endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, and hypercoagulability.

  1. Endothelial injury — exposes subendothelial collagen & tissue factor, denudes antithrombotic surface, releases vWF. Platelets adhere via GP Ib-IX-V and are activated. Tissue factor activates the extrinsic coagulation cascade. Dominant in cardiac & arterial thrombi — atherosclerotic plaque rupture (MI), traumatic / catheter injury, vasculitis, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, cigarette smoking.
  2. Abnormal blood flow
    • Stasis — pool of blood allows activated clotting factors to accumulate; removes dilution effect; common in deep vein thrombosis (immobilisation, surgery, heart failure, AF, post-stroke). Sluggish venous flow also reduces endothelial clearance of activated factors.
    • Turbulence — damages endothelium at arterial bifurcations, aneurysms, around atherosclerotic plaques, prosthetic valves; causes platelet-endothelium interaction and counter-currents that favour coagulation.
  3. Hypercoagulability
    • Primary (genetic) — Factor V Leiden (most common), prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin III deficiency, protein C & S deficiency, dysfibrinogenaemia.
    • Secondary (acquired) — malignancy (Trousseau), pregnancy, OCPs, prolonged bed rest, surgery, trauma, burns, nephrotic syndrome, antiphospholipid syndrome, myeloproliferative neoplasms, homocysteinaemia, older age, obesity, smoking.

Most clinical thrombi arise from a combination of all three — e.g. a post-operative elderly patient with cancer and immobilisation has stasis + hypercoagulability + endothelial trauma from intravenous cannula.

Clinical Pearl

Stasis favours venous thrombi (red, fibrin-rich, do not propagate toward heart); endothelial injury favours arterial thrombi (white, platelet-rich). Recognition of which element predominates guides antithrombotic choice — antiplatelets for arterial, anticoagulants for venous.
q0_0_3_1:
Reversible Cell Injury

Reversible injury is the early stage of cell damage — cellular & functional alterations that can recover if the offending stimulus is removed. Two key targets are ATP depletion and membrane integrity.

Mechanisms

  1. Hypoxia / ischaemia → decreased oxidative phosphorylation → ↓ ATP.
  2. Failure of Na+/K+-ATPase → intracellular Na+ accumulation, K+ loss → cellular swelling (hydropic change), endoplasmic reticulum dilation.
  3. Switch to anaerobic glycolysis → ↑ lactate, ↓ intracellular pH → clumping of nuclear chromatin.
  4. Detachment of ribosomes from rough ER → ↓ protein synthesis → lipid deposition in injured cells (fatty change — especially in liver, heart).
  5. Ca2+ influx — ATP-depleted pumps fail to extrude Ca2+; mild rise activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases.
  6. ROS generation — at low levels can be detoxified; oxidative stress damages lipids, proteins, DNA.

Morphological Changes

  • Gross — pallor, swelling, increased weight, soft consistency.
  • Light microscopy
    • Cellular swelling (hydropic change) — earliest change.
    • Fatty change — triglyceride accumulation (steatosis).
    • Pigments — lipofuscin, haemosiderin, melanin.
  • EM (ultrastructure)
    • Plasma membrane blebbing.
    • Loss of microvilli.
    • Mitochondrial swelling & amorphous densities.
    • Dilation of ER with detachment of ribosomes.
    • Nuclear chromatin clumping.

Clinical Pearl

The key event that converts reversible to irreversible injury is severe mitochondrial dysfunction with MPTP opening, ATP depletion below the threshold for Na+/K+ pump, and profound membrane damage — leading to cell death by necrosis and/or apoptosis.
q0_0_3_2:
Role of Free Radicals in Cell Injury

Free radicals are chemical species with an unpaired electron in the outer orbit — highly reactive, initiate autocatalytic chain reactions. Major ROS in biology: superoxide anion (O2·−), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), hydroxyl radical (·OH), peroxynitrite (ONOO−).

Sources

  • Endogenous — mitochondrial electron transport chain ( leakage); phagocyte oxidase during respiratory burst; peroxisomes; enzymes (xanthine oxidase in ischaemia-reperfusion; NADPH oxidase; cytochrome P450; NO synthase).
  • Exogenous — radiation (UV, ionising), oxygen toxicity (hyperbaric), chemicals (CCl4 → CCl3·), drugs (acetaminophen, doxorubicin, bleomycin), cigarette smoke, environmental pollutants, reperfusion after ischaemia.

Mechanisms of Injury

  1. Lipid peroxidation — radical attacks polyunsaturated fatty acids in membranes → destruction of membrane integrity, formation of malondialdehyde (MDA) & 4-HNE.
  2. Protein damage — oxidation of sulfhydryl groups, cross-linking, fragmentation → loss of enzyme activity & structural protein function.
  3. DNA damage — strand breaks, base modification (8-oxo-guanine) → mutagenesis, activation of p53 → apoptosis.
  4. Mitochondrial damage — opening of mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP), cytochrome-c release → apoptosis; ATP depletion → necrosis.
  5. Activation of stress signalling — NF-κB, MAP kinases, inflammasome → cytokine release, inflammation.

Antioxidant Defence

  • Enzymatic — superoxide dismutase (SOD; O2·− → H2O2), catalase (H2O2 → H2O + O2), glutathione peroxidase (uses GSH).
  • Non-enzymatic — vitamin E (lipid membranes), vitamin C (aqueous), β-carotene, uric acid, bilirubin, glutathione, transferrin, ceruloplasmin.

Clinical Pearl

Ischaemia–reperfusion injury is the classic example — restoration of blood flow after ischaemia brings oxygen that fuels xanthine oxidase & mitochondrial electron leak, generating ROS that worsen tissue injury. This explains the benefit of early reperfusion in MI / stroke but also the paradox of reperfusion arrhythmias and stunning.
q0_0_3_3:
Mechanisms of Tumour Metastasis

Metastasis is the spread of tumour cells from the primary site to distant organs, forming secondary tumours. It is the hallmark of malignancy and accounts for >90% of cancer deaths.

Pathway

  1. Local invasion — tumour cells detach (loss of E-cadherin), degrade basement membrane & extracellular matrix via matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-2, MMP-9), and migrate (autocrine motility factors, integrins, chemokine receptors such as CXCR4).
  2. Intravasation — tumour cells enter capillaries / venules / lymphatics.
  3. Transport — circulated as single cells or emboli coated with platelets & fibrin (protects from shear stress & NK cells).
  4. Arrest & adhesion — bind to endothelium at distant site via selectins, integrins, CD44; site specificity dictated by chemokine gradients ("seed & soil" hypothesis — Paget).
  5. Extravasation — exit the vessel into the parenchyma.
  6. Survival & angiogenesis — survive in foreign microenvironment ("metastatic niche" primed by exosomes); induce angiogenesis (VEGF, FGF) to support growth into clinically detectable metastasis.
flowchart TD A[Primary tumour] --> B[Local invasion - MMP, loss of E-cadherin] B --> C[Intravasation into vessel] C --> D[Circulation as emboli] D --> E[Arrest in distant capillary] E --> F[Extravasation] F --> G[Survival in new microenvironment] G --> H[Angiogenesis & growth] H --> I[Clinical metastasis]

Routes of Spread

  • Lymphatic — carcinomas (regional nodes first).
  • Haematogenous — sarcomas, RCC (renal vein), HCC, lung, melanoma, choriocarcinoma; liver, lung, bone, brain.
  • Transcoelomic — ovarian (Krukenberg from stomach), gastric (Blumer shelf, Sister Mary Joseph nodule).
  • CSF / leptomeningeal — medulloblastoma, leukaemia, breast, lung.
  • Seeding of body cavities — thoracic, peritoneal, pericardial.
  • Iatrogenic — along biopsy tract, surgical wound.

Clinical Pearl

Seed and soil hypothesis (Paget, 1889) explains why different tumours metastasise to specific organs — breast to bone, lung, liver, brain; colorectal to liver; prostate to bone (osteoblastic); RCC to bone, lung (cannonball), thyroid to bone. Pre-metastatic niche is "prepared" by tumour exosomes & bone-marrow-derived cells.
q0_0_3_4:
Anaphylaxis — Why within Minutes

Anaphylaxis is a Type I (immediate / IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction that develops within minutes (typically 5–30 min) of exposure to an allergen. The rapid time-course is dictated by the fact that the immune response is pre-formed — IgE is already bound to mast cells & basophils from prior sensitisation.

Mechanism

  1. Prior sensitisation — initial exposure to allergen (bee venom, peanut, drug, latex) → B-cell class-switching → production of allergen-specific IgE → binds FcεRI receptor on mast cells & basophils. No clinical reaction at first exposure.
  2. Re-exposure — allergen cross-links adjacent IgE molecules on the mast cell surface within seconds.
  3. Signal transduction — FcεRI aggregation activates Lyn & Syk tyrosine kinases → PLCγ → IP3 & DAG → Ca2+ release & PKC activation.
  4. Immediate (within seconds-minutes) — mast-cell degranulation releases preformed mediators stored in granules: histamine, tryptase, chymase, heparin, serotonin. These cause:
    • Vasodilation & increased vascular permeability → hypotension, urticaria, angioedema, laryngeal oedema.
    • Bronchoconstriction → wheeze, respiratory distress.
    • ↑ mucus secretion, ↑ gut motility → cramps, vomiting, diarrhoea.
  5. Late-phase (4–8 h) — newly synthesised lipid mediators (leukotrienes LTC4/D4/E4, prostaglandin D2, platelet-activating factor) and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) recruit eosinophils & basophils — late recrudescence of symptoms.
flowchart TD A[Prior sensitisation → IgE bound to mast cell FcεRI] --> B[Re-exposure to allergen] B --> C[Cross-linking of IgE] C --> D[FcεRI signalling → Ca2+] D --> E[Immediate: histamine, tryptase, heparin release] E --> F[Vasodilation, bronchospasm, oedema within minutes] D --> G[Late phase: leukotrienes, PGD2, PAF, cytokines] G --> H[Eosinophil & basophil recruitment 4-8 h later]

Clinical Pearl

IM injection of adrenaline (0.5 mg, 1:1000) at the anterolateral thigh is the first-line treatment and is most rapidly absorbed because of the high vascularity and large muscle mass. Repeat every 5 min if no response. Patient should be observed for ≥6 h because of biphasic reactions in 5–20% of cases.
q0_0_3_5:
Septic Shock & Multi-Organ Failure

Septic shock is a subtype of distributive shock characterised by systemic vasodilation, hypotension, and tissue hypoperfusion despite adequate fluid resuscitation, caused by an uncontrolled host response to infection. Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) results when this cascade becomes self-sustaining.

Pathogenesis

  1. Trigger — microbial products (LPS / endotoxin of gram-negative bacteria; lipoteichoic acid of gram-positive; superantigens of S. aureus / S. pyogenes) bind pattern-recognition receptors (TLR4, TLR2, CD14).
  2. Cytokine storm — macrophages, monocytes & endothelium release TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12, IFN-γ, HMGB1. These produce fever, hypotension, acute-phase response.
  3. Endothelial activation & dysfunction — ↑ adhesion molecules (ICAM, VCAM, E-selectin); ↑ NO (iNOS) → vasodilation & hypotension; ↑ permeability → capillary leak → tissue oedema & hypovolaemia; loss of glycocalyx → microvascular thrombosis.
  4. Coagulopathy — tissue factor expression → DIC; consumption of platelets & clotting factors; microvascular thrombi → tissue ischaemia.
  5. Mitochondrial dysfunction — "cytopathic hypoxia": cells cannot utilise oxygen even when delivered — oxygen extraction ratio falls; lactate rises. NO & H2S inhibit cytochrome c oxidase.
  6. Myocardial depression — circulating myocardial depressant factors (TNF, IL-1, NO) → reduced contractility → worsens hypotension.
  7. Organ failure — kidneys (AKI), lungs (ARDS), liver (jaundice, synthetic failure), brain (encephalopathy), heart (cardiomyopathy), gut (ileus, translocation), adrenals (relative adrenal insufficiency), coagulopathy, immune paralysis (compensatory anti-inflammatory response syndrome, CARS).
flowchart TD A[Infection: LPS / TLR4] --> B[Cytokine storm TNF, IL-1, IL-6] B --> C[iNOS → NO → Vasodilation, hypotension] B --> D[Endothelial leak → oedema, hypovolaemia] B --> E[Tissue factor → DIC → microthrombi] B --> F[Mitochondrial dysfunction → cytopathic hypoxia] B --> G[Myocardial depression] C --> H[Tissue hypoperfusion] D --> H E --> H F --> H G --> H H --> I[Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome]

Clinical Pearl

The qSOFA score (altered mentation, systolic BP ≤100, respiratory rate ≥22) identifies high-risk patients outside ICU. Early goal-directed therapy ( Surviving Sepsis Campaign "hour-1 bundle") — antibiotics within 1 h, 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, lactate, vasopressors to MAP ≥65 mm Hg — has reduced sepsis mortality substantially.

FeatureReversibleIrreversible
ATP depletionModest; cell survives if O2 restoredSevere; cannot be reversed
Membrane integrityIntactSeverely damaged — key event
MitochondriaSwollen, amorphous densitiesMPTP opening, cytochrome-c release → apoptosis; massive swelling → rupture
Cellular swellingReversible hydropic changeMassive swelling; membrane blebs rupture
NucleusChromatin clumpingPyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis
LysosomesIntactRupture → enzyme leakage → autolysis
Calcium influxMild, reversibleMassive Ca2+ influx → enzyme activation, cell death
Recovery on removing stimulusYesNo
OutcomeReturn to normal or steatosisNecrosis and/or apoptosis

Key Determinants

  • Mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP) — sustained opening is the "point of no return".
  • Loss of membrane phospholipids — due to phospholipase A2 activation; compromises ion transport & osmotic regulation.
  • Cytoskeletal damage — leads to membrane bleb rupture and loss of intracellular contents.
  • Genetic programme — if cell has intact apoptotic machinery, ATP depletion triggers apoptosis; if ATP is profoundly depleted, necrosis predominates.

Clinical Pearl

In myocardial infarction, the ischaemic myocardium is reversibly injured for ~20–30 min, after which necrosis begins. This is why the cardinal principle of acute MI management is "time is muscle" — early reperfusion (PCI <90 min, thrombolysis <30 min) salvages myocardium that would otherwise die.
q0_0_3_7:
Pathogenesis of SLE

SLE is a chronic multisystem autoimmune disease driven by a triad of (1) autoantibody production, (2) immune complex formation, and (3) tissue deposition with complement activation.

  1. Genetic susceptibility — HLA-DR2/DR3, complement deficiencies (C1q, C2, C4) impair clearance of immune complexes & apoptotic bodies.
  2. Trigger — UV light, drugs, infection → keratinocyte apoptosis with exposure of nuclear antigens (DNA, histones, Ro, La).
  3. Defective clearance of apoptotic material — germinal-centre macrophages fail to clear debris → persistence of nuclear antigens.
  4. Polyclonal B-cell activation with loss of tolerance → autoantibodies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Ro/La, anti-phospholipid). T-helper cells provide help via BAFF over-production.
  5. Type III hypersensitivity — antigen-antibody complexes form in circulation, deposit in glomeruli (mesangium & subendothelium), serosa, skin (dermo-epidermal junction), vessel walls → complement activation (low C3/C4), Fc-receptor-mediated inflammation → glomerulonephritis, serositis, vasculitis.
  6. Type II hypersensitivity — antibodies against cell-surface antigens cause haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia.
  7. Antiphospholipid antibodies — lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin — cause a prothrombotic state (vascular thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy loss).
flowchart TD A[Genetic + trigger UV] --> B[Apoptosis → nuclear antigen exposure] B --> C[Defective clearance] C --> D[Autoreactive B/T activation] D --> E[Autoantibodies ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm] E --> F[Immune complexes → Type III] F --> G[Glomerulonephritis, serositis, vasculitis] E --> H[Anti-cell surface → Type II] H --> I[Cytopenias] E --> J[Antiphospholipid Ab → thrombosis]

Clinical Pearl

Anti-dsDNA titres track disease activity and nephritis; low complement (C3, C4) confirms active immune-complex disease. Anti-Sm is the most specific antibody for SLE.
q0_0_3_8:
Pathogenesis of Primary (AL) Amyloidosis

AL amyloidosis results from over-production of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (usually λ) by an expanded plasma-cell clone, which misfold into β-pleated sheet fibrils and deposit in tissues.

  1. Clonal plasma-cell disorder — >80% of AL arises in association with multiple myeloma, smouldering myeloma, MGUS, or rarely B-cell lymphoma. A small, low-burden clone can produce enough light chain to cause systemic amyloidosis even without overt myeloma.
  2. Overproduction of free light chains — λ (70%) more amyloidogenic than κ. Bone-marrow plasma cells (often <10%) secrete monoclonal light chain that appears in serum as a peak on serum free light chain assay (altered κ:λ ratio).
  3. Misfolding & proteolysis — light chains undergo conformational change from normal immunoglobulin fold to β-pleated sheet. Variable-region fragments are resistant to proteolysis; partial cleavage by macrophage proteases yields the amyloidogenic fragment.
  4. Fibrillogenesis — misfolded monomers oligomerise into 7.5–10 nm rigid, non-branching fibrils; serum amyloid P (SAP) and glycosaminoglycans bind & stabilise the fibrils, preventing breakdown.
  5. Tissue deposition — fibrils deposit in extracellular space of heart (restrictive cardiomyopathy), kidney (nephrotic syndrome), liver (hepatomegaly), nerves (sensorimotor & autonomic neuropathy), tongue (macroglossia), skin, GI tract & vasculature.
  6. Organ dysfunction — physical disruption of architecture, direct light-chain toxicity to cardiomyocytes, & vascular deposition cause restrictive cardiomyopathy, nephrotic-range proteinuria & orthostatic hypotension.
flowchart TD A[Clonal plasma cells in marrow] --> B[Overproduction of monoclonal free light chain λ] B --> C[Misfolding to β-pleated sheet] C --> D[Proteolytic cleavage by macrophages] D --> E[Oligomerisation → 7.5-10 nm fibrils] E --> F[SAP & GAG stabilisation] F --> G[Extracellular tissue deposition] G --> H[Heart, kidney, nerve, liver, tongue damage]

Clinical Pearl

Macroglossia + periorbital purpura + nephrotic-range proteinuria + restrictive cardiomyopathy (low ECG voltages with thick ventricular walls) is pathognomonic of AL amyloidosis. Treat the underlying clone with bortezomib-based therapy; amyloid regression follows clone suppression.

q0_0_3_10:
Pathogenesis of Tubercle

A tubercle (granuloma) is the diagnostic histological lesion of tuberculosis, formed by the immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Sequence of Events

  1. Inhalation of droplet nuclei (1–5 µm) containing 1–10 bacilli → reach alveoli (lower lobe / apical segment of upper lobe — high oxygen tension).
  2. Phagocytosis by alveolar macrophages — bacilli resist killing due to complement-mediated uptake avoiding respiratory burst; sulfatides & lipoarabinomannan (LAM) inhibit phagosome-lysosome fusion.
  3. Intracellular multiplication → macrophage death → release of bacilli & antigen.
  4. Acute inflammation (3–7 days) — neutrophils & fresh macrophages accumulate; bacilli spread to regional lymph nodes (Ghon focus).
  5. Acquired cellular immunity (2–3 weeks) — dendritic cells migrate to draining lymph nodes, present antigen on MHC-II to naive CD4+ T cells → Th1 differentiation under IL-12. Th1 cells release IFN-γ → macrophage activation; CD8+ T cells kill infected macrophages.
  6. Granuloma formation — activated macrophages transform into epithelioid cells (abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries) and Langhans giant cells (peripheral horseshoe arrangement of nuclei). Lymphocytes (CD4+) rim the periphery.
  7. Caseation necrosis — central amorphous eosinophilic debris (named because of cheese-like gross appearance) — due to IFN-γ-mediated macrophage activation & TNF-α, tissue necrosis, lipid-loaded cell death.
  8. Fibrosis & calcification — at the periphery; collagen deposition, eventually calcify; bacilli survive within caseous material but dormant.
flowchart TD A[Inhalation of droplet nuclei] --> B[Alveolar macrophage phagocytosis - phagosome-lysosome blocked] B --> C[Bacillus multiplies → macrophage death] C --> D[Antigen spread to lymph node → Th1 response] D --> E[IFN-γ activation of macrophages] E --> F[Epithelioid cells + Langhans giant cells + lymphocyte rim = granuloma] F --> G[Central caseous necrosis] G --> H[Fibrosis & calcification]

Clinical Pearl

The Ghon complex (subpleural focus + hilar lymph node granuloma) is the primary TB lesion in children; calcified Ghon complex visible on chest X-ray is the "Ghon lesion". Reactivation TB occurs in apex of upper lobe (high O2) — forms a "Simon focus".
q0_0_3_11:
Pathogenesis of Malaria

  1. Transmission — bite of female Anopheles mosquito (40+ species vectors) injectes sporozoites from salivary glands into human blood.
  2. Pre-erythrocytic (hepatic) schizogony — sporozoites reach liver within 30 min; invade hepatocytes; undergo asexual division over 7–10 days to form schizonts containing 10,000–30,000 merozoites (hypnozoite stage in P. vivax / P. ovale causes relapse). Hepatocyte ruptures, releasing merozoites. No clinical symptoms at this stage.
  3. Erythrocytic schizogony — merozoites bind erythrocyte receptors (Glycophorin A — P. falciparum; Duffy antigen — P. vivax; Duffy-negative protects). Ring trophozoite → mature trophozoite → schizont → rupture, releasing 8–32 merozoites (cycle 48 h for P. vivax/ovale/falciparum; 72 h for P. malariae); cycles synchronised → fever spikes (tertian vs quartan).
  4. Gametocytogenesis — some merozoites differentiate into male & female gametocytes (banana-shaped in falciparum); taken up by mosquito, undergo sporogony in mid-gut → sporozoites migrate to salivary glands → infectious.
  5. Pathophysiology — haemolysis (malaria pigment haemozoin released), anaemia, splenomegaly, cytokine release (TNF-α, IFN-γ) causing fever. In P. falciparum, PfEMP-1 protein on infected RBC causes cytoadherence to endothelial CD36, ICAM-1; rosetting & sequestration in deep microvasculature (cerebral malaria, placental malaria, ARDS, renal failure, blackwater fever — intravascular haemolysis, haemoglobinuria).
flowchart TD A[Anopheles bite → sporozoites] --> B[Hepatic schizogony 7-10 d] B --> C[Merozoites] C --> D[Erythrocytic cycle: ring → trophozoite → schizont → merozoites] D --> E[Periodic fever] C --> F[Gametocytes] F --> G[Mosquito ingests → sporogony] G --> A D --> H[PfEMP1 cytoadherence → cerebral malaria, ARDS, AKI]

Diagnostic Criteria

  • Clinical — fever with chills & rigors, periodicity, splenomegaly, anaemia in endemic area.
  • Microscopy (gold standard) — thick + thin peripheral blood smear, stained with Giemsa; species ID & parasite density.
  • RDT — HRP-2 (falciparum), pLDH, aldolase.
  • PCR — low parasitaemia, mixed infection.
  • Supportive — anaemia, thrombocytopenia, raised reticulocyte count, jaundice, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia (especially falciparum), raised creatinine.

Clinical Pearl

Severe falciparum malaria: impaired consciousness/cerebral malaria, convulsions, prostration, respiratory distress (acidosis), jaundice, haemoglobinuria, severe anaemia (Hb <5), hypoglycaemia, AKI, DIC, parasitaemia >2% — give IV artesunate immediately.

q0_0_3_13:
Routes of HIV Transmission

  1. Sexual (most common worldwide)
    • Heterosexual (main mode in sub-Saharan Africa & India — 85% of new infections)
    • Homosexual / bisexual (MSM — commonest in North America & Western Europe)
    • Risk ↑ with STDs (especially ulcerative — syphilis, chancroid, herpes), cervical ectopy, ano-genital trauma, multiple partners, lack of circumcision
    • Viral load is the strongest determinant — risk ∝ plasma & genital viral load
  2. Blood & blood products
    • Transfusion of infected whole blood, packed cells, platelets, factor VIII/IX (now rare — screened)
    • Needle-stick injury — occupational risk ~0.3% percutaneous, 0.09% mucous membrane
    • Sharing needles / syringes among IV drug users (high efficiency — 0.67% per act)
    • Unsterile medical injections, tattooing, acupuncture, razors at barber shop
  3. Maternal-to-child transmission (MTCT / vertical)
    • In-utero (10%) — transplacental, especially if mother has high viral load
    • Intra-partum (65%) — exposure to maternal blood & cervical secretions during vaginal delivery
    • Post-partum (25%) — breastfeeding (risk ~10–20% over 18 months)
    • Without intervention MTCT rate ~15–45%; with full PPTCT (ART + elective LSCS + no breastfeeding + infant NVP) <2%
  4. Organ / tissue transplantation — kidney, liver, heart, cornea, bone, skin (donor screening now mandatory)
  5. Artificial insemination, surrogacy with unscreened donor semen

Not transmitted by — casual contact (hug, handshake), sharing utensils, mosquito bites, saliva, sweat, tears, urine, faeces, swimming pool, toilet seat.

Clinical Pearl

Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) within 72 h of exposure reduces infection risk by >80% — start 3-drug regimen (TDF + 3TC/FTC + DTG) for 28 days. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with TDF/FTC daily reduces sexual acquisition by ~99% in high-risk MSM and serodiscordant couples.
q0_0_3_14:
Mechanisms of Tumour Metastasis

Metastasis is the multi-step spread of tumour cells from the primary site to a distant organ where they establish a secondary growth. It is the hallmark of malignancy and accounts for >90% of cancer deaths.

Steps

  1. Detachment — loss of E-cadherin, decreased cell-cell adhesion; cells gain motility.
  2. Local invasion — secretion of matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-2, MMP-9) degrades basement membrane & extracellular matrix; tumour cells migrate via autocrine motility factors, integrins & chemokine receptors (CXCR4).
  3. Intravasation — tumour cells penetrate capillary / venular / lymphatic wall.
  4. Transport — circulate as single cells or homotypic/heterotypic emboli coated with platelets & fibrin (protection from NK cells & shear stress).
  5. Arrest & adhesion — bind to endothelium at distant site via selectins, integrins, CD44, L1-CAM. Specificity dictated by chemokine gradients (seed & soil — Paget).
  6. Extravasation — exit vessel into parenchyma (paracellular or transcellular).
  7. Survival & angiogenesis — adapt to foreign microenvironment (metastatic niche primed by tumour exosomes & bone-marrow-derived cells); induce angiogenesis via VEGF, FGF; grow into clinically detectable metastasis.

Routes

  • Lymphatic — carcinomas first (regional nodes → distant nodes); melanoma; seminoma.
  • Haematogenous — sarcomas, RCC (renal vein → IVC → lung), HCC (hepatic vein), lung, melanoma, choriocarcinoma. Common sites: liver, lung, bone, brain.
  • Transcoelomic — ovarian (Krukenberg from stomach), peritoneal seeding, pleural seeding.
  • CSF / leptomeningeal — medulloblastoma, ependymoma, leukaemia, lymphoma, breast, lung.
  • Seeding of body cavities — thoracic, pericardial, peritoneal (ascites).
  • Iatrogenic — along biopsy tract, surgical wound.

Clinical Pearl

Some patterns are classic — Virchow node (left supraclavicular — abdominal malignancy stomach, pancreas, testis); Sister Mary Joseph nodule (umbilical metastasis — gastric, ovarian, colon); Krukenberg tumour (ovarian metastasis — stomach, colon, breast); Blumer shelf (rectal shelf from gastric cancer).

Always classify amyloid by both chemistry (AL vs AA vs ATTR) and distribution (systemic vs localised). LMD/MS (laser microdissection/mass spectrometry) is the modern gold standard — replaces older immunohistochemistry-based typing, which sometimes mislabels ATTR as AL due to non-specific binding.

Pathological Changes in Candidiasis

Candida albicans and related species are dimorphic fungi — yeast in tissue, pseudohyphae in chronic/deep infection. Lesions vary by site and host immune status.

Histological Patterns

  • Acute superficial candidiasis (oral thrush, vaginal, oesophageal in HIV)
    • White creamy pseudomembrane of desquamated epithelial cells, fibrin, neutrophils & fungal elements — easily scraped off (vs leukoplakia which cannot).
    • Underlying mucosa erythematous, oedematous with neutrophilic infiltrate.
    • PAS or GMS stain shows budding yeast cells (3–6 µm) & pseudohyphae invading superficial epithelium.
    • Microabscesses in squamous epithelium with budding yeast & neutrophils (so-called "neutrophilic microabscesses").
  • Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis — chronic plaque / hyperkeratotic lesions; marked parakeratosis, acanthosis, intra-epithelial neutrophils; persistent yeast forms in stratum corneum; seen in T-cell deficiency, AIRE / STAT1 mutations, thymoma.
  • Systemic / invasive candidiasis
    • Multiple microabscesses in kidney, liver, spleen, brain, heart, retina, lung.
    • Renal — cortical microabscesses ("fungal nephritis"), papillary necrosis.
    • Cardiac — endocarditis (large friable vegetations), myocardial microabscesses.
    • Cerebral — microabscesses, glial nodule.
    • Ocular — chorioretinitis with white cotton-wool retinal lesions, vitreous clouding ("string of pearls").
    • Skin — generalized maculopapular rash ("candida rash" in neutropenic / disseminated).
    • Bone — osteomyelitis, septic arthritis.
  • Candidaemia — fever, chills, sepsis; IV cannulae and neutropenia are risk factors; retinal lesions are a clue.

Special Stains & Culture

  • PAS (pink-magenta), Gomori methenamine silver (GMS — black), Calcofluor white (fluorescence).
  • Culture — Sabouraud dextrose agar; germ-tube test for C. albicans; chromogenic agar for species; automated blood culture systems.
  • β-D-glucan serum assay — broad marker; useful in invasive candidiasis.

Clinical Pearl

persistent oral candidiasis in an adult without obvious cause (dentures, antibiotics, steroids) is an AIDS-defining illness — send HIV test. Pseudohyphae + budding yeast on KOH mount confirm; germ-tube positive within 90 min at 37°C confirms C. albicans.
q0_0_3_17:
Rb Gene — Tumour Suppressor Mechanism

The retinoblastoma (RB1) gene on chromosome 13q14 was the first tumour-suppressor gene discovered. It encodes pRB, a 110-kDa nuclear phosphoprotein that controls the G1→S transition of the cell cycle.

Two-Hit Hypothesis (Knudson)

  • Familial retinoblastoma — one mutant RB1 allele inherited in germline; second hit (somatic) inactivates the remaining allele in retinal cell → bilateral multifocal retinoblastoma in young children; ↑ risk of osteosarcoma later in life.
  • Sporadic retinoblastoma — two somatic hits in same retinal cell → unilateral, unifocal, later onset.

Mechanism of Action

  1. In G0/early G1, pRB is hypophosphorylated and binds E2F family of transcription factors, sequestering them. E2F cannot transcribe S-phase genes (cyclin E, cyclin A, DHFR, thymidine kinase, DNA polymerase α).
  2. When mitogenic signals (growth factor → Ras → MAPK) arrive, cyclin D is induced; cyclin D-CDK4/6 complex phosphorylates pRB.
  3. Further phosphorylation by cyclin E-CDK2 in late G1 → hyperphosphorylated pRB → releases E2F.
  4. Free E2F activates S-phase gene transcription → cell cycle progresses through restriction point.
  5. pRB is dephosphorylated by PP1 during mitosis, restoring its inhibitory form for next cycle.

Loss of Function → Cancer

  • Loss-of-function mutation of both RB1 alleles → E2F constitutively free → uncontrolled S-phase entry → tumorigenesis.
  • In cancers without RB1 mutation, the pathway is often disabled by other means — overexpression of cyclin D1 (parathyroid adenoma PRAD1, mantle cell lymphoma t(11;14)), CDK4 amplification (melanoma), or inactivation of p16INK4a (CDKN2A) inhibitor (pancreatic, melanoma, NSCLC).
  • HPV E7 protein binds & degrades pRB → cervical cancer; SV40 large T, adenovirus E1A similarly inactivate pRB.
flowchart TD A[Growth factor] --> B[Cyclin D / CDK4-6] B --> C[pRB phosphorylation] C --> D[E2F release] D --> E[S-phase genes → DNA replication] F[p16 INK4a inhibitor] -. blocks .-> B G[HPV E7] -. degrades .-> H[pRB] G --> I[Uncontrolled E2F → cancer]

Clinical Pearl

The "pRB pathway" — p16 / cyclin D / CDK4 / pRB / E2F — is disrupted in essentially every human cancer. Loss of p16 (e.g. by mutation, deletion, promoter hypermethylation) is the most common alteration of the pathway in solid tumours. CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib) restore the brake in ER+ breast cancer.
q0_0_3_18:
Coagulative vs Liquefactive Necrosis — Why Different in MI vs Cerebral Infarct

The pattern of necrosis is determined by the tissue's protein content, enzymatic environment, and lipid content.

Myocardial Infarction — Coagulative Necrosis

  • Myocardium is a highly specialised tissue rich in contractile proteins (actin, myosin) and structural proteins.
  • Ischaemia → ATP depletion → irreversible injury & cell death; structural protein framework denatures & coagulates, but remains intact as a "ghost" outline of the cell.
  • Lysosomal enzymes are inactivated by the acidic intracellular pH and low temperature of underperfused tissue.
  • Result — firm, pale, wedge-shaped area; microscopic — eosinophilic anucleate cells with preserved outline; neutrophils infiltrate at margin by 12–24 h.
  • Healing — phagocytosis of debris by neutrophils & macrophages, granulation tissue by day 7, scar by 4–6 weeks.

Cerebral Infarction — Liquefactive Necrosis

  • Brain tissue has very little structural protein (no collagenous stroma between neurons) but high lipid content and abundant lysosomal enzymes.
  • Ischaemic death triggers release of lysosomal hydrolases from neurons & glia; enzymatic digestion of tissue liquefies the necrotic brain.
  • Microglia & infiltrating neutrophils release proteases — matrix is digested, tissue becomes soft, semiliquid.
  • Result — initially pale, soft, swollen; later cystic cavity forms (days-weeks), surrounded by gliosis.
  • Bacterial infection in brain (abscess) also liquefies — same mechanism.
FeatureCoagulative (MI)Liquefactive (Brain)
TissueHigh protein, low lipid, low lysosomeHigh lipid, low structural protein, high lysosome
Lysosomal enzymeInactivated by acidosisActive — digestion continues
OutcomeCell outlines preserved; firm scarTissue liquefies; cystic cavity

Clinical Pearl

Exceptions: in the brain, the only exception to liquefactive necrosis is tuberculoma — which shows caseous (cheesy) necrosis. In other organs, coagulative is the rule for ischaemia; liquefactive for bacterial abscess. Fat necrosis (acute pancreatitis) and caseous (TB) are distinct morphological variants.
q0_0_3_19:
Septic Shock — Warm then Cold Extremities

The clinical progression from "warm shock" to "cold shock" reflects the haemodynamic evolution of septic shock.

Early / Warm Shock (Hyperdynamic Phase)

  • Massive cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IFN-γ) → upregulation of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) in vascular smooth muscle & endothelium.
  • ↑ NO production → systemic arteriolar vasodilation (SVR ↓↓) → warm, dry, flushed extremities; bounding pulse; wide pulse pressure.
  • Capillary leak → relative hypovolaemia; heart compensates with tachycardia & high cardiac output (CI >4 L/min/m²).
  • Cellular dysoxia — extraction ratio falls; lactate rises despite pink, well-perfused appearance ("warm, but sicker than they look").
  • Oxygen delivery is high but mitochondrial oxygen utilisation is impaired ("cytopathic hypoxia").

Late / Cold Shock (Hypodynamic Phase)

  • Persistent capillary leak & third-space loss → progressive hypovolaemia.
  • Myocardial depression by circulating myocardial depressant factors (TNF, IL-1, NO) → reduced contractility → cardiac output falls.
  • Microvascular dysfunction — DIC, microthrombi, endothelial swelling → patchy tissue ischaemia.
  • Loss of vasomotor tone, depleted catecholamine reserve, possible relative adrenal insufficiency.
  • Cool, clammy, mottled, cyanotic extremities; weak thready pulse; oliguria, altered mentation.
  • Cold shock: SVR may be high or low; CI low (<2.5 L/min/m²).
  • Multi-organ dysfunction — AKI, ARDS, liver failure, DIC, coma.
flowchart LR A[Sepsis → cytokine storm] --> B[iNOS ↑ → NO ↑] B --> C[Vasodilation → warm shock] C --> D[Capillary leak → hypovolaemia] C --> E[Myocardial depression] D --> F[Cardiac output ↓ → cold shock] E --> F F --> G[Multi-organ failure]

Clinical Pearl

The transition from warm to cold shock indicates decompensation — high mortality. Early recognition (qSOFA, lactate) & aggressive resuscitation within the "golden hour" (antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors to MAP ≥65 mm Hg) prevents this transition.

Fat Embolism Syndrome

The likely diagnosis is fat embolism syndrome (FES) following a long-bone fracture.

Pathophysiology

  • Mechanical theory — disruption of medullary veins & bone in long-bone (esp. femur, tibia, pelvis) fractures releases fat globules into venous circulation → lodge in pulmonary, cerebral & systemic capillaries (after traversing patent foramen ovale or pulmonary shunts).
  • Biochemical / free-fatty-acid theory — lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses neutral fat to free fatty acids & inflammatory mediators (thromboxane, prostaglandins) → endothelial damage, platelet activation, complement cascade → capillary leak, ARDS, microvascular thrombosis.
  • Manifestations within 24–72 h of injury — classic triad:
    1. Respiratory distress — dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, ARDS-like picture (most common & earliest).
    2. Neurological symptoms — confusion, agitation, seizures, coma, focal deficits (cerebral fat embolism).
    3. Petechial rash — over chest, axillae, conjunctivae, retina — pathognomonic but present in only ~50–60%.
  • Other features — fever, tachycardia, thrombocytopenia, anaemia, lipuria, fat droplets in sputum & urine.

Diagnosis

  • Clinical — major (petechial rash, respiratory distress, cerebral dysfunction) and minor (fever, tachycardia, jaundice, renal dysfunction, thrombocytopenia, fat in urine/sputum) criteria (Gurd's criteria).
  • Chest X-ray — bilateral diffuse alveolar / interstitial infiltrates.
  • CT brain — diffuse white-matter petechial haemorrhages ("starfield" pattern).
  • Bronchoalveolar lavage — fat droplets in macrophages (suggestive).
  • Echocardiography — may show right heart strain.

Clinical Pearl

Early surgical fixation of long-bone fractures (within 24 h) reduces FES risk substantially. Treatment is supportive — high-flow oxygen, mechanical ventilation with lung-protective strategy, haemodynamic support. Corticosteroids are controversial but may help if given prophylactically in high-risk patients.
q0_0_3_21:
Reversible Tubular Cell Injury — Why Recovery?

The clinical scenario describes pre-renal azotaemia due to dehydration, which produced reversible ischaemic cell injury — the tubular cells recovered because damage had not yet crossed the threshold to irreversible necrosis (acute tubular necrosis, ATN).

Mechanism of Recovery

  1. Injury was hypoxic, not cytotoxic — pure dehydration causes reduced renal blood flow & GFR; tubular cells become hypoxic but not exposed to a directly cytotoxic agent (e.g. mercuric chloride, gentamicin).
  2. ATP depletion was partial — sufficient ATP remained to maintain plasma-membrane Na+/K+-ATPase, lysosomal integrity & cytoskeleton. Membrane blebs formed but did not rupture; mitochondrial permeability transition pore did not sustainably open.
  3. Reversibility window — in ischaemic renal injury, tubular cells develop sub-lethal changes (cellular swelling, brush-border blunting, mitochondrial swelling) but recover if perfusion is restored before membrane rupture.
  4. Tubular cells are labile (or stable) — renal proximal tubular epithelium has regenerative capacity; once perfusion & oxygenation are restored, surviving cells re-enter cell cycle & repopulate the tubule within days to weeks.
  5. Reperfusion re-energises ATP-dependent repair — Na+/K+-ATPase restores cell volume, Ca2+ pump reduces cytosolic calcium, oxidative phosphorylation resumes, protein synthesis restarts.
  6. Low oxygen demand of tubular cells in medullary portion — the medulla has limited blood supply but medullary tubular cells have adapted to relative hypoxia; some tolerance buys time.

When Would Necrosis Have Occurred?

  • If hypoperfusion persisted beyond ~30–60 min (or if additional insults — sepsis, nephrotoxin, contrast, rhabdomyolysis).
  • If severe ATP depletion triggered MPTP opening → apoptosis; if membranes ruptured → necrosis. Both manifest clinically as ATN — more prolonged AKI (1–3 weeks), granular casts, FENa >2%, and slower recovery.

Clinical Pearl

Distinguish pre-renal AKI (BUN:Cr >20, FENa <1%, urine osmolality >500) from intrinsic ATN (BUN:Cr <15, FENa >2%, muddy brown casts, osmolality <350). The former is rapidly reversible with volume resuscitation; the latter requires supportive care until tubular regeneration occurs.
q0_0_3_22:
Acute Appendicitis — Pathological Basis of Symptoms

The four cardinal signs of acute appendicitis (redness, swelling, pain, fever) correspond directly to the classical features of acute inflammation — rubor, tumor, dolor, calor — first described by Celsus.

  1. Redness (rubor)
    • Luminal obstruction (faecolith, lymphoid hyperplasia, parasite) → bacterial overgrowth → mucosal injury & release of inflammatory mediators (histamine, prostaglandins, bradykinin).
    • Arteriolar vasodilation → ↑ blood flow → visible redness of serosa at laparoscopy/laparotomy.
    • Histamine & leukotrienes cause increased vascular permeability — protein-rich exudate.
  2. Swelling (tumor)
    • Vascular congestion & exudation of fluid into the appendiceal wall → oedema.
    • Neutrophilic infiltrate of mucosa → muscularis → serosa; pus in lumen; gross — appendix enlarged, turgid, engorged.
    • Exudate may extend to peritoneal surface → fibrinous exudate → localised peritonitis.
  3. Pain (dolor)
    • Initially visceral pain — dull, poorly localised, periumbilical — because the midgut-derived appendix refers pain to T10 dermatome.
    • As inflammation extends to parietal peritoneum (somatic afferents), pain shifts to right iliac fossa (McBurney point) — sharp, localised, worse on movement / coughing.
    • Bradykinin, prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2), substance P, and serotonin sensitise nociceptors → hyperalgesia.
  4. Fever (calor)
    • Macrophages & neutrophils release IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α → prostaglandin E2 in hypothalamus → upward reset of body thermostat.
    • Low-grade fever (37.5–38.5°C) typically; high fever & rigors suggest perforation / peritonitis / septicaemia.

Other Signs

  • Nausea, vomiting — visceral afferent stimulation.
  • Tachycardia — fever & cytokines.
  • Rebound tenderness, Rovsing sign, psoas sign, obturator sign — parietal peritoneal irritation.

Clinical Pearl

Migratory pain from periumbilical to right iliac fossa + anorexia + low-grade fever + localised peritoneal signs (McBurney tenderness, Rovsing, rebound) — the classic presentation. Operate early; delay risks perforation and generalized peritonitis, especially in young children & the elderly.
q0_0_3_23:
Nephrotic Oedema — Mechanism Despite Normal Heart

In nephrotic syndrome, massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/1.73 m²/day) triggers a sequence of events that leads to generalised oedema — entirely independent of cardiac function.

Pathogenesis — Starling Forces Altered

  1. Hypoalbuminaemia — urinary loss of albumin (>3.5 g/day) exceeds hepatic synthesis → serum albumin falls <2.5 g/dL → reduced plasma oncotic pressure.
  2. Decreased oncotic pressure — fluid shifts from intravascular to interstitial compartment (Starling forces: net filtration ↑).
  3. Intravascular volume depletion — decreased effective circulating volume is sensed by juxtaglomerular apparatus → renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) activation.
  4. Secondary hyperaldosteronism — ↑ aldosterone → sodium & water reabsorption in distal tubule → further volume expansion; despite RAAS, oncotic pressure remains low → reabsorbed fluid leaks into interstitium → worsening oedema.
  5. ADH release — non-osmotic ADH secretion (response to "underfill") → free-water reabsorption → dilutional hyponatraemia.
  6. Sodium retention by primary renal mechanism — even with "overfill" theory, damaged glomeruli & tubular cells have reduced ability to excrete sodium — decreased GFR, increased proximal & distal Na+ reabsorption.
  7. Capillary leak — hypoalbuminaemia, oxidative stress & circulating factors in nephrotic state increase capillary permeability — worsens oedema.
  8. Generalised oedema — periorbital (worst in morning), dependent (ankles, sacrum), ascites, pleural effusions, genital swelling; severe cases — anasarca.
flowchart TD A[Glomerular damage → massive proteinuria >3.5 g/d] --> B[Hypoalbuminaemia] B --> C[↓ Plasma oncotic pressure] C --> D[Fluid shifts to interstitium → oedema] C --> E[↓ Effective circulating volume] E --> F[RAAS activation → Na+ & H2O retention] E --> G[Non-osmotic ADH → free water retention] F --> H[Increased plasma volume → still low oncotic pressure → more oedema] G --> H A --> I[Decreased GFR & renal Na+ excretion] I --> H

Clinical Pearl

Nephrotic oedema is typically periorbital and worse in the morning (vs cardiac oedema which is dependent & worse in the evening). Treat the underlying disease (steroids for minimal-change disease, ACE-inhibitor/ARB for proteinuria, diuretics with care — risk of intravascular depletion due to low oncotic pressure — combine loop + albumin in severe cases).
